title: COMP/MCCAA/13/2023 – Assessment of Proposed Acquisition by Lidl Immobiliare Malta Limited of Property at Żabbar Belonging to Said Investments Limited to operate Lidl Supermarket (Phase 2 Decision)
text:

Zabbar Belonging to Said Investments Limited to operate Lidl Supermarket unlawful in terms

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1. The Office for Competition within the Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority has
opened an in-depth investigation to assess whether the proposed acquisition by Lidl Immobiliare
Malta Limited (Purchaser) of properties at Zabbar belonging to Said Investments Limited (Vendor)
and leases belonging to Scotts Limited (Tenant) is in line with the Control of Concentrations
Regulations (Subsidiary Legislation 379.08).
2. If the parties’ request is acceded by the Office for Competition, Lidl Immobiliare Malta Limited will
be acquiring the Scotts supermarket in Zabbar and the adjacent portion of land currently used as
a parking area by Scotts supermarket from Said Investments Limited with the intention of
eventually leasing it out to Lidl Malta Limited to operate a ‘Lidl’ supermarket.
3. In the local geographic market, within a 15-minute drive, Lidl's post-concentration market share is
highly probable to reach [], notwithstanding Eurospin achieving its projected market share. HHI
values exceeding 2,000 and a high delta indicate increased market concentration.
4. The Office considers that in the local geographic market:
i. Lidl is already leading and has a significant presence in the market, acquiring the Scotts
Zabbar store would further solidify the Lidl’s market share. This change would further
widen the gap between Lidl and its closest competitors, exacerbating the imbalance in
the competitive landscape.
ii. Lidl’s market share has remained stable over the years, and thus, the acquisition would
further consolidate its high market share. Even a small increase in market share for a
strong player like Lidl could reinforce its strong position, reducing the competitive
pressures in the market. This is particularly important in the context that Lidl’s market
share has been stable over the years.
iii. Lidl’s already high market share, combined with the addition of Scotts Zabbar’s market
share, would result in a market share that is appreciably larger than that of the largest
competitor. This would solidify Lidl’s market position and harm competition by making
it harder for other competitors to challenge Lidl’s market presence effectively.
Considering Lidl’s high market shares that have remained stable over several years
this could indicate potential dominance.
iv. The HHI and the delta increase resulting from this concentration are above the
thresholds. This indicates an SLC. The high HHI and delta values underscore the
potential for reduced market competition in the context of limited number of
competitors, further justifying the rejection of Lidl’s acquisition of the Scotts Zabbar
store.
5. Furthermore, uncertainty around Eurospin’s opening date implies that Lidl could have a substantial
period to solidify its market position before facing new competition, heightening SLC concerns.
Even with Eurospin’s entry into the market, the SLC concerns would persist due to Eurospin’s
relatively low market share.
6. The GUPPI test suggests the concentration could reduce consumer welfare, allowing Lidl to raise
prices. However, the other market players still offer competitive terms, exerting some form of
constraint on Lidl. Nonetheless, the market shares would exceed [], creating or strengthening a
dominant position.
Office for Competition - 5 -

7. Lidl’s expansion efforts in the local geographic market, including pending development approvals,
signal an intent to strengthen its market share and create barriers to entry, deterring potential
competitors due to the scarcity of suitable commercial spaces in the local geographic market.
8. The Office concludes that the proposed concentration will lead to SLC, limiting competition in the
local grocery retail market. The horizontal unilateral effects could harm competition and consumer
welfare both currently and in the future.
9. The Office finds that, the proposed transaction infringes regulation 4(1) and in terms of regulation
8(3) is issuing this decision and is declaring that the proposed concentration is unlawful in terms
of the Control of Concentrations Regulations (LN 294 of 2002 as Subsequently Amended).
Office for Competition - 6 -

1. INTRODUCTION
1.1. Background
1. On 29 December 2023, the Office for Competition within the Malta Competition and Consumer
Affairs Authority (hereinafter referred to as “the Office”) initiated proceedings for an in-depth
investigation in accordance with regulation 6(1)(iii) of the Control of Concentrations
Regulations.
2. In this investigation, the Office needs to appraise whether the proposed concentration will lead
to a substantial lessening of competition in the grocery retail market.
3. This requires that the Office assesses the effect the proposed acquisition will have on
competition. By consistently posing a threat of losing existing business to competitors,
competition compels businesses to remain responsive to customer demands and adapt to
market needs. A substantial lessening of competition occurs when rivalry becomes
considerably less intense following a concentration, leading to a suboptimal outcome for
customers, such as higher prices, lower quality, inferior after-sales service, or limited choice.
4. This decision, together with its appendices, constitutes the Office’s findings, whereby the
Office is blocking the proposed acquisition by Lidl Immobiliare Malta Limited of Property at
Zabbar Belonging to Said Investments Limited.
5. Throughout this report, the Office refers to Lidl Malta Limited and Scotts Limited collectively
as “the Parties”, and Lidl Malta Limited as the “Notifying Party”.
1.2. Facts
6. On 24 August 2023, a Promise of Sale Agreement was duly signed between Said Investments
Limited (Vendor) and Scotts Limited (Tenant), and Lidl Immobiliare Malta Limited (Purchaser)
to purchase the Zabbar Properties with operational permits and with vacant possession. The
Parties agreed that the Promise of Sale Agreement shall remain valid and effective up to and
including 24th February 2024. The Proposed Transaction follows another proposed
transaction dated 22 March 2023 which relates to both the Promise of Sale Agreement for the
purchase of the Zabbar Properties and the Promise of Assignment of Lease Agreements for
the assignment of leases of Attard, Santa Lucia, and Naxxar properties between Lidl
Immobiliare Malta Limited and Said Investments Limited. The transaction of 22 March 2023
was later abandoned by the Parties.
7. Following a number of meetings convened between the Office for Competition and the
Notifying Party, the concentration notification form was deemed complete on Tuesday 14
November 2023. The period between the date of the agreement and the notification of the
concentration exceeds the fifteen working days stipulated in regulation 5(1) of the Control of
Concentrations Regulations. However, the extension of the time period was acceded to by
the Director General of the Office for Competition.
8. The filing and the acceptance of the concentration notification was notified to the public
through a public notice in the Government Gazette (No. 21,152) on Friday 17 November 2023
and a notice that appeared in a local newspaper and on the Malta Competition and Consumer
Affairs Authority’s website on the same day.1
9. In compiling the competitive assessment, the Office for Competition has relied extensively on
relevant guidelines issued by the European Commission, European competition case law,
and previous decisions issued by the Office for Competition in the Maltese grocery retail
sector. These include the Phase II decision issued by the Office for Competition on 5 June
1 Invitation to Comment < https://mccaa.org.mt/media/8794/invitation-for-third-parties-to-comment-lidl-scotts-Żabbar-property-
november-2023.pdf > last accessed 25 November 2023, 17 November 2023.
Office for Competition - 7 -

2020 concerning the full-function joint venture between Retail Marketing Limited and Co-op
Trading Company Limited, Polrem Limited, S. Borg & Sons Limited, Tower Supermarkets
Complex Limited, Valyou Pendergardens Operations Limited, Belleview Supermarkets
Company Limited and Valyou Supermarket Limited,2 the Phase II decision issued by the
Office for Competition on 9 June 2021 concerning the acquisition by Lidl Immobiliare Malta of
some of the buildings belonging to Said Investments Limited and leases belonging to Scotts
Limited to operate ‘Lidl’ supermarkets from them,3 and the Phase I decision issued by the
Office for Competition on 10 November 2021 in relation to the proposed acquisition by Lidl
Immobiliare Malta Limited of property at Zabbar belonging to Said Invetsments Limited to
operate Lidl supermarket.4 The former concentration concerned the Maltese grocery retail
market and involved analysing the market competitive environment pre- and post the
integration of the operational activities of four established local supermarket chains,
collectively operating eight retail supermarkets and one convenience shop in Malta. The latter
concentration concerned the same sector in Malta and involved the same parties to this
proposed concentration, whereby the Office analysed the competitive situation pre- and post-
acquisition of these Parties.
10. On 17 November 2023, the Office published an invitation for third parties to put forward their
objections on the proposed concentration.5 Pursuant to regulation 5(4) of the Control of
Concentrations Regulations the Office for Competition has also published the invitation on the
Government Gazette and a local newspaper on the same day. To guarantee wide outreach
on 17 November 2023, the Office also sent an email to grocery retail outlets inviting them to
submit their comments on the proposed concentration. Four third-party objections were
received.
11. In evaluating the Zabbar proposed concentration in 2021 (COMP/MCCAA/11/2021) by the
same Parties, the Office deemed it important to analyse both the demand-side and supply-
side aspects. The demand-side (consumer) perspective is considered important for the
following reasons: (i) it plays a crucial role in accurately defining and delineating the retail
grocery market in Malta, (ii) it ensures that the competitive evaluation is grounded in the local
context, rather than relying exclusively on European case law, and (iii) it guarantees that the
decision made by the Office for Competition is reflective of the current market dynamics rather
than being rooted in conjecture and counterfactuals driven by subjective elements. On the
other hand, when examining the supply-side perspective, specifically focusing on grocery
retail outlets, the Office for Competition is drawing upon two key sources of data: (i) third-party
objections raised against the proposed concentration, and (ii) Requests for Information sent
to all grocery retail outlets in Malta. These requests primarily cover data pertaining to store
market size, turnover, average sales per customer, selling prices of various branded products,
the breadth of product offerings across diverse food and beverage categories, and additional
inquiries related to services such as advertising programmes, customer service standards,
and loyalty schemes, among others.
12. As of 23rd November 2023, in light of the absence of publicly accessible information regarding
the supply-side grocery retail market in Malta, the Office for Competition issued a Request for
Information to grocery retail outlets in Malta, in accordance with Regulation 10 of the Control
of Concentrations Regulations.
13. The demand-side analysis involved conducting an exit store survey at the Scotts Zabbar
outlet, aiming to provide a more precise quantification of the impact of the acquisition on
competition. In this regard, on 1st December 2023, a Call for Quotes was issued by the Office
for the provision of services in relation to the exit store survey in Zabbar. Evaluating the

Company Ltd., Polrem Ltd., S. Borg & Sons Ltd., Tower Supermarkets Complex Ltd., Valyou Pendergardens Operations Ltd.,
Belleview Supermarkets Co. Ltd. and Valyou Supermarket Ltd (Phase II Decision).
3 Case COMP/MCCAA/13/2020 - Assessment of proposed acquisition by Lidl Immobiliare Malta Limited of some of the

Office for Competition - 8 -

demand-side perspective is important not only for understanding the prevailing consumer
trends but also for gaining insights into consumer behaviour.
14. On 29 December 2023, the Office initiated proceedings for an in-depth investigation in
accordance with regulation 6(1)(iii) of the Control of Concentrations Regulations. In this
decision, the Office expressed serious doubts regarding the compatibility of the proposed
concentration with the Regulations and believes that the proposed acquisition could
substantially limit competition in the grocery retail market. Primarily, the proposed
concentration could lead to horizontal unilateral effects, both existing and future constraints,
harming competition and consumer welfare in the process.
15. The Promise of Sale Agreement was extended on the 22nd February 2024 up to 30th June
2024, and then again up until the end of August 2024.
16. On 24th May 2024, Lidl submitted commitments to address the provisional substantial
lessening of competition should the proposed transaction materialise. The Office did not
consider that the proposed commitments sufficiently and suitably address the competition
concerns arising from the proposed transaction, by Lidl (Purchaser) to acquire properties at
Zabbar belonging to Said Investments Limited (Vendor).
17. The Notifying Party was notified with a Statement of Objections pursuant to regulation 16(1)(b)
on the 25th July 2024. On the same day, access to the file of the investigation was provided
to the Notifying Party pursuant to regulation 16(4) (a). On the 20th August 2024, the Office
received a reply to the Statement of Objections. The Notifying Party had the opportunity to
develop the arguments verbally on the 27th August 2024 pursuant to regulation 16(1) (c).
18. The Promise of Sale was extended again up until 13th September 2024, and again up until
4th October 2024.
2. THE PARTIES AND THE NATURE OF THE TRANSACTION
2.1. The Parties
19. Lidl is a German discount chain belonging to the Schwarz Group, a German-based retailer
operating 12,000 stores in 31 countries, with a worldwide turnover of EUR154.1 billion in 2022.
The first Lidl store to open its doors in Malta was in Santa Venera in 2008. Since then, the
company expanded further and today counts ten supermarkets, in Mosta, San Gwann, Qormi,
Luqa, Safi, Zejtun, Santa Venera, Gozo, and more recently in Sliema and Burmarrad.
20. In fact, following the decision of the Office for Competition on 9 June 2021, Lidl Malta Limited
was granted permission to purchase two divided undeveloped portions of land in Attard, the
Burmarrad outlet and lease rights to the portion of land situated near Scotts Supermarket in
Burmarrad and leased by Scotts Limited as a parking area for cars, and the lease to the
supermarket outlet in Sliema from Said Investments Limited. Moreover, on 26 August 2021,
the Planning Authority issued a permit for Lidl Malta Limited to expand its operations in
Żebbuġ (Malta) in the site currently occupied by SMW Cortis, while a permit for a proposed
supermarket in the former General Soft Drinks Complex in Qormi (Malta) has been approved
on the 12th September 2024. As a result, apart from this concentration, Lidl Malta Limited will
be expanding its number of outlets to eleven supermarkets in the short-term, possibly to
twelve if Lidl develops another supermarket outlet in Qormi.
21. In Malta, Lidl operates through three companies: Lidl Malta Limited (C 36317), Lidl
Immobiliare Malta Limited (C 36321) (hereinafter “the Notifying Party”) and Lidl Logistica
Malta Limited (C 79620), all having their registered address at The Vassallo Business Park,
Burmarrad Road, Naxxar, NXR 6345, Malta. Lidl Malta Limited’s principal activity is to operate
supermarkets and retail outlets for the sale of finished and packaged products relating to
Office for Competition - 9 -

foodstuffs, beverages and allied products, and household items. On the other hand, Lidl
Immobiliare Malta Limited is a property company responsible for acquiring immovable
property and plant and machinery for leasing in its ordinary cause of operations. Lidl Logistica
Malta Limited holds and operates a logistics hub. All companies are part of the same group
structure, with the Lidl Italia S.r.l being the majority shareholder.
22. The turnover of Lidl Malta Limited for the financial year ended 28 February 2022 was circa.
EUR[] million (2021: approx. EUR[] million). This puts Lidl Malta Limited as the leader in
Malta’s grocery retail sector in terms of turnover. Through its current ten stores, Lidl Malta
Limited boasts a total sales area of around [] square meters and on average employed
around [] employees during the year ended 28 February 2022 (2021: [] employees). The
company generated a profit after tax of circa. EUR[] million (2021: approx. EUR[] million)
for the financial year ending 28 February 2022. The current existing sales floor area of Lidl in
Malta is [] square meters.
23. The other parties to the concentration are Said Investments Limited (hereinafter “the Target”)
and Scotts Limited. Said Investments Limited is a limited liability company registered in Malta
with company registration number C13285 and registered address at The Said Buildings,
Fleur de Lys Road, Birkirkara, Malta. Said Investments Limited is a property company whose
objectives include purchasing and acquiring immovable property in Malta and the carrying on
of the business as operator and administrator in connection with the properties that it
purchases and acquires.
24. Scotts Limited is a limited liability company registered in Malta with company registration
number C33305 and the same registered address of Said Investments Limited. Scotts Limited
acts as an importer and retailer of finished products relating to foodstuffs, beverages and
allied products, and household items.
25. Scotts Limited opened its doors in 2002 with the first grocery supermarket located in Naxxar.
Scotts Limited expanded further by opening seven other grocery retail outlets throughout the
years, in Attard, Burmarrad, Santa Lucija, Sliema, Zabbar, Birkirkara and Spinola, before
closing the Spinola outlet in January 2019, and selling the Sliema and Burmarrad outlets to
Lidl Immobiliare Malta Limited in June 2021. The Santa Lucija outlet was closed on 6th May
2024. The turnover of Scotts Limited was circa. EUR[] million in 2022 (2021: approx.
EUR[] million). The total sales area of Scotts Limited is estimated around [] square
meters in 2022, when excluding the Sliema and Burmarrad outlets.
2.2. Nature of the Transaction
26. The proposed concentration is the acquisition by Lidl Immobiliare Malta Limited of properties
at Zabbar (as better defined hereinafter) belonging to Said Investments Limited and leases
belonging to Scotts Limited (hereinafter after “the Proposed Transaction”).
27. On 24 August 2023, Lidl Immobiliare Malta Limited entered into a Promise of Sale agreement
with Said Investments Limited to acquire the Zabbar Properties comprising of a complex
without official number in Triq il-Mina ta’ Hompesch in Zabbar, with a superficial area of
approximately 6,020 square metres consisting of:
a. the building used as a supermarket, without official number known as “Scotts” formerly
known as “Sisa” and formerly known as “Pirella Supermarket” and prior to that as
“Corrigo Hall Wedding Complex”, in Triq il-Mina ta’ Hompesch in Zabbar, which building
in part underlies third party property; of the outside areas include the out-buildings
without number which are accessible by a driveway which forms an integral part of this
complex and which also provides access to the Zabbar parking area, which driveway
measures approximately five hundred and five square metres (505sq.m.) and is
bounded on the east in part by the remainder of this complex and in part by the Zabbar
parking area, on the south by Triq il-Mina ta’ Hompesch and on the north by the
property of [[]] or of his successors in title; which entire complex is bounded on the
south by Triq il-Mina ta’ Hompesch, on the north east by the Zabbar parking area and
Office for Competition - 10 -

on the north by property of [[]] or of his successors in title as defined by the existing
boundary walls and which complex includes all and any improvements made thereon
and all its rights and appurtenances including the overlying airspace and the underlying
terrain.
b. the divided portion of land of a rectangular shape known as “Tal-Mandarin” in the limits
of Zabbar, surrounded on all sides with a boundary wall which segregates it from
adjacent properties, which land is used as a parking area of the Zabbar Supermarket
and has a superficial area of not less than three thousand four hundred square metres
(3,400sq.m.), bounded on the north west by property of [[]], on the south west in part
by property of [[]] or his successors in title and in part by the Zabbar Supermarket to
which it is interconnected and in part by property of the Government of Malta and on
the west by property of [[]] or other variable boundaries.
28. The Parties to the concentration agree that the Zabbar Properties will be sold tale quale in
their current state and condition, with all their rights and appurtenances, including the
overlying airspace and their underlying terrain. The Zabbar Properties will be transferred with
vacant possession upon the signing of the Deed of Sale.
29. The Parties to the concentration agree that their intention is to transfer the Zabbar properties
as a stand-alone asset. According to the Notifying Parties to the concentration, it is not the
intention for Lidl Immobiliare Malta Limited and/or Lidl Malta Limited to acquire the business
that is carried out by Scotts Limited from the Zabbar Properties. The transaction therefore
excludes the transfer of any going concern, personnel, goodwill, intellectual property,
tradenames or trademarks, trade secrets and/or customer databases, etc. Furthermore,
nothing in the Promise of Sale and /or the Deed of Sale shall be interpreted or construed so
as to create or impose any sort of limitation or prohibition on how the Vendor (Said
Investments Limited) or the Tenant (Scotts Limited) conduct their business in the future, and
accordingly Said Investments Limited and/or Scotts Limited may perform any act of business
or trade, including those which may be in competition with the business or trade of the
Purchaser.
30. The Promise of Sale agreement is conditional on the Office, declaring the transaction a lawful
concentration in terms of the Control of Concentration Regulations. The proposed
concentration is not subject to review by any other competition authority.
2.3. Third-Party Objections
31. On 17 November 2023, the Office notified for general information that it received a notification
of a proposed concentration between Said Investments Limited (Vendor, Birkirkara, Malta)
and Scotts Limited (Tenant, Birkirkara Malta), and Lidl Immobiliare Malta Limited (Purchaser,
Luqa Malta) to purchase Zabbar Properties, belonging to Said Investments Limited and leases
belonging to Scotts Limited with operational permits and with vacant possession. The
concentration notification was notified to the public through a public notice in the Government
Gazette (No. 21,152) and a notice that appeared on the Malta Competition and Consumer
Affairs Authority’s website and in a local newspaper on the same day. In that notification, the
Office invited interested parties to submit their comments on the proposed concentration.
Furthermore, the Office for Competition also sent an email to grocery retail outlets inviting
them to submit their comments on the proposed concentration.
32. The Office received four third party submissions in total, all raising concerns about the
proposed concentration. The views submitted by third parties reflect a range of views on Lidl’s
relative position compared to its competitors.
33. In summary, the main issues relate to the fact that concentration will lead to a substantial
lessening of competition, which will bring about negative consequences for both the business
community and consumers. A summary is provided in the next subsections.
Office for Competition - 11 -

2.3.1. Lidl’s Dominant Position
34. In general, third parties claim that Lidl has a dominant position in the product market and will
continue to consolidate its position. Indeed, respondents stated that Lidl Malta’s size is a
significant concern, especially since its market share has continued to increase over these
years of operations. Its market share is expected to continue to increase, considering the

3.1. Jurisdiction
63. The mission statement of the Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority is “the
attainment and maintenance of well-functioning markets for the benefit of consumers and
economic operators”.6 To this end, the Authority is entrusted with a number of functions

amongst which is “to promote and enhance competition”.7 This function is carried out by the

3.2. Counterfactual
72. In accordance with regulation 4 of the Control of Concentrations Regulations, the Office shall
consider the following factors in its assessment of concentrations, among others:
a. the need to maintain and develop effective competition in the
Maltese market in view of, among other things, the structure of all
the markets concerned and the actual or potential competition from
undertakings located either within or outside Malta;
b. whether the business, or part of the business, of a party to the
concentration has failed or is likely to fail;
c. the nature and extent of development and innovation in a relevant
market; and
d. the market position of the undertakings concerned and their
economic and financial power, the alternatives available to suppliers
and users, their access to supplies or markets, any legal or other
barriers to entry, supply and demand trends for the relevant goods
and services, the interests of the intermediate and ultimate
consumers, and the development of technical and economic
progress provided that it is to consumers’ advantage and does not
form an obstacle to competition.
73. Concentrations leading to efficiency gains surpassing and counterbalancing any competition-
related drawbacks shall not be prohibited, provided the involved undertakings can
demonstrate that these efficiency gains cannot otherwise be attained, are verifiable and likely
to be passed on to consumers in the form of lower prices, or greater innovation choice or
quality of products or services.
74. In accordance with Horizontal Merger Guidelines, in order to evaluate the effects of the
transaction, the Office conducts a counterfactual analysis by “compar[ing] the competitive
conditions that would result from the notified merger with the conditions that would have
prevailed without the merger.”9
75. The term “counterfactual” refers to the hypothetical situation where the concentration does
not occur. If the Office finds that the hypothetical scenario without the concentration is
substantially more favourable for competition compared to the actual concentration scenario
(“the factual”), it shall object to the proposed transaction unless the involved parties offer
adequate remedies.
9 See Guidelines on the assessment of horizontal mergers under the Council Regulation on the control of concentrations
between undertakings (“Horizontal Merger Guidelines”), 2004 OJ C31/5, para. 9.
Office for Competition - 17 -

76. In order to identify the adverse effect, or harm, resulting from a decrease in competition and
the associated risks, the Office takes into account relevant data and bases its assessment on
a plausible economic scenario. Only the situation prior to the concentration can be observed
and the probable effects of the concentration can only be assumed. While the assessment is
primarily grounded in the characteristics of the relevant market and its competitive dynamics
at the time of the evaluation, it also considers potential future developments. This includes
prospective factors like market entry, exit or expansion.10 The Horizontal Merger Guidelines
express this principle in the following terms that the assessment “may take into account future
changes to the market that can reasonably be predicted. It may, in particular, take account of
the likely entry or exit of firms if the merger did not take place when considering what
constitutes the relevant comparison.”11 The appropriate counterfactual may increase or
reduce the prospects of a substantial lessening of competition (hereinafter “SLC”) finding by
the Office.
77. In formulating a plausible economic scenario for assessing the effects of a concentration, the
Office integrates anticipated shifts in market structure into its analysis. This is especially
relevant when such changes are deemed reasonably probable given the current market
landscape. Hence, if reliable information suggests the potential entry, expansion, or exit of a
market player, we factor this into our competition evaluation over and above the prevailing
market conditions scenario, i.e., the counterfactual scenario. Additionally, when determining
the credible counterfactual scenario, we consider not only the prevailing market conditions
but also the financial capabilities of the relevant undertaking and its involvement in adjacent
markets.
78. The scope of counterfactual analysis is not intended to forecast the market at a specific
moment in time. Rather, the goal is to develop plausible and realistic counterfactuals that
serve as a benchmark for assessing the actual market outcomes. Any counterfactual
competitive dynamics considered by the Office must align with and adhere to competition law.
79. The determination of the counterfactual is not aimed at ossifying the market at a specific
moment. By way of example, an assessment considering the current competitive landscape
might suggest that, in the absence of the concentration under consideration, the involved
parties would have persisted in making investments in enhancements, innovations, or new
products. Here, only events that would have taken place without the concentration being
considered – and are not a result of it – can be included in the counterfactual.
80. The Office will choose the most probable competitive conditions as the basis for comparison
against which the concentration would be assessed. The Office may have to consider various
scenarios before deciding on the appropriate basis of comparison. In doing so, the Office shall
determine if any of the possible scenarios have a significant impact on the competitive
conditions. If so, the Office shall choose the most likely conditions of competition in the
absence of the concentration as the counterfactual.
81. Establishing the suitable counterfactual to evaluate a concentration is a task that carries
inherent uncertainty, and it may be challenging to gather evidence related to future
developments that could happen if the concentration does not materialise. However, this
uncertainty about the future does not necessarily mean that the Office will automatically
assume that the situation before the concentration is the appropriate counterfactual. As part
of this assessment, and following a series of RFIs to the Parties and third-parties, the Office
considers the following factors as relevant over and above the prevailing market conditions:
a. expansion by one of the Parties;
b. the exiting firm scenario; and
c. entry or expansion of competitors in the market.
10 See, e.g., Case T-342/00, Petrolessence SA et al v. Commission, 2003 ECR II-1161, para. 102.
11 Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paras. 76-88.
Office for Competition - 18 -

82. Expansion by one of the Parties: The Office considers whether, in a scenario where the
concentration had not taken place, one of the Parties would have expanded. For example, if
any party to the concentration plans to expand in the existing relevant market, the Office shall
assess evidence related to the likelihood of the Parties expanding their operations. This
evidence may include direct indications of their intentions to expand, such as insights into
their broader operational strategy. Additionally, the Office may consider any past instances of
situations where any party to the concentration showed strong intentions to expand and the
reasons for failing to do so. However, the Office will also consider the timeliness and strength
of expansion, and if it would be sufficient for the proposed concentration to give rise to an
SLC, in its competitive assessment. The Office also considers that expansion would also have
to be sufficiently realistic.
83. Exiting firm scenario: The Office considers whether, absent the concentration, one of the
Parties to the concentration is likely to have exited the market. In forming a view on an existing
firm scenario, the Office will consider whether (i) the firm is likely to have exited (through failure
or otherwise); and, if so (ii) there would not have been an alternative, less anti-competitive
purchaser for the firm or its assets to the acquirer in question. The exiting firm scenario is
typically evaluated when one of the firms is believed to be struggling financially. Nonetheless,
exit may also occur for a variety of other reasons, such as a shift in the business strategy of
the undertaking. The Office acknowledges that the financial position of the firm on its own
may not be sufficient to demonstrate that exit is inevitable or likely.
84. Entry or expansion of competitors in the market: The Office acknowledges that the entry
of third parties in the market, and their potential expansion, are important factors in the
counterfactual scenario. However, in such a case, the counterfactual scenario is not meant to
be an exhaustive description of the competitive environment that would exist without the
proposed transaction. The Office recognises that significant changes affecting competition
from third parties would occur with or without the concentration, and form a part of the
counterfactual, does not usually merit to assess them in detail as part of the counterfactual
assessment. Nonetheless, given the expected changes of the grocery retail market in Malta,
the Office conducted a thorough examination of the current market conditions and consulted
with third parties about their future plans. These considerations were then incorporated into
the competitive assessment outlined in this assessment.

but also be of a scale that can effectively compete with the Notifying Party. Without timely and
sufficient market entry, the assessment may conclude that competition will be significantly
weakened by the proposed transaction. Additionally, the new entrant must be a credible player
with a strong name, ideally with a proven history in the market. This credibility ensures that
the entrant can attract customers and pose a substantial competitive constraint. Moreover,
the new entrant must offer a similar PQRS to effectively challenge the Notifying Party. Without
a credible name, past market experience, and a comparable PQRS offering, the market entry
may not be sufficient to maintain competitive pressure.

4. OVERVIEW OF THE MALTESE RETAIL GROCERY SECTOR
120. The food retail industry plays a crucial role in providing consumers with access to a wide range
of food products. It encompasses a broad range of stores and outlets, including supermarkets,
discounters, convenience stores, online retail platforms and independent food specialist
stores (such as butchers and vegetable hawkers) that are either independent businesses or
part of larger networks.
121. The core business activity of the notifying parties is the sale of groceries. For the purposes of
this decision, this includes food and beverages sold by grocery retailers, as well as toiletries,
home care products, and similar items.32 Based on annual turnover figures for 2022, the
Notifying Party has the highest turnover value in Malta among grocery retail stores. Indeed,
in 2022, the Notifying Party recorded a turnover figure of nearly €[] million, equivalent to a
market share of []%.33 Alongside core groceries, the Notifying Party also sell items such
as electronic equipment, clothing and personal care items, which constitute around []% of
their total turnover. On the other hand, during the same year, Scotts recorded an annual
turnover figure of nearly €[] million, equivalent to a market share of []%.
4.1. Importance of grocery retailing
122. Grocery retailing is a critical industry because of its significant size and the provision of
essential items to Maltese households. Retail stores operating within this industry do not
manufacture or produce goods, although in some cases, they slightly modify products, e.g.,
in-store preparation of meat, cooking, baking, retail packaging of salads, etc.
123. Based on the National Accounts data published by the National Statistics Office (NSO), in
2022, Maltese households spent around €1,105.8 million on food and non-alcoholic
beverages and €272.2 million on alcoholic beverages and tobacco. Indeed, the total spent on
food, beverages and tobacco stood €208.7 million (or an increase of 17.8%) higher in 2022
than it was in 2021 due to a two-pronged effect: volume base effects as Malta strongly

124. The latest figures from the Household Budgetary Survey also show that food and non-
alcoholic beverages account for almost one-fifth of Maltese households’ total spending. Meat
is the largest share of their food and non-alcoholic expenditure on which households spent
the largest share of their expenditure (21.2%), followed by fruit and vegetables (20.2%), bread
and cereals (16.7%), milk, cheese and eggs (13.6%), and non-alcoholic beverages (10.1%).
The share of alcoholic beverages and tobacco accounts for 2.4% of total household
consumption. However, some households spend much more on food and non-alcoholic
beverages. For example, in the case of one- and two-person households, it accounts for
nearly 22%. Moreover, the expenditure share on food and non-alcoholic beverages is also
significantly higher for households within the first income quintile (25.6%) than those with an
income in the fifth quintile (16.1%). Thus, a significant loss of competition in the grocery retail
market will significantly impact Maltese households, particularly vulnerable ones.
125. COVID-19 invariably impacted the economic and consumer sentiment. While consumption of
food and beverages was negatively affected due to the closure of the airport, bars, pubs,
social clubs, and nightclubs, post-pandemic periods were characterised by a spike in pent-up
demand, especially in 2022, as Malta resumed its usual operations. Indeed, during the
COVID-19 pandemic, households resorted to essential commodities and less on impulse
buying.35 Household members spent more time indoors, resulting in a shift in consumption
from on-trade (such as bars) to off-trade (such as supermarkets).36
126. COVID-19 also affected the way people conduct their grocery shopping. During the height of
the pandemic, governments resorted to social distancing and lockdown measures to attenuate
its spread. These measures led to changes in shopper behaviour across the grocery retail
market, especially online shopping. However, primary data collected by the Office for
Competition for this decision reveals that post-pandemic, most respondents reverted to a
traditional in-person shopping experience for groceries, and only a minor share of people
maintained online shopping patterns for groceries in 2022.
4.2. Grocery retail channels
127. In general, the following terminology in the food retail industry is accepted to distinguish
between different types of food retailers:37
a. Hypermarkets: a store with a sales area of over 2,500 square meters with at least 35%
of selling space devoted to non-food items. Sometimes, hypermarkets are also called
“superstores”, a combination of a supermarket and a department store. Hypermarkets
are usually located in the suburbs due to the limited space availability in city centres
and the need for large parking areas for shoppers. Sometimes, hypermarkets are
located close to residential areas and can be adjacent to shopping centres that sell
consumer electronics, furniture, durable and leisure goods, etc.
b. Supermarket: a store with typically 400 to 2,500 square meters of sales area with at
least 70% of its selling space dedicated to food products.
c. Discounters: stores that typically have a sales area of 300–900 square meters, have
less than 1,000 product lines (predominantly packaged food and non-food products),
and sell products at prices lower than those of traditional retail stores. Goods in

discount stores usually have own-label or budget brands. Aldi, Lidl, Netto, and Eda are
well-known examples of this type of retail outlet.
d. Convenience Stores: these stores sell a wide range of goods and have extended
opening hours. They are often located alongside busy roads, near gas stations, railway
stations, or in densely populated urban areas. Product selection is limited compared
with supermarkets, and in many stores, only one or two choices are available for each
type of product. Prices in convenience stores are typically higher than in supermarkets.
e. Independent Grocers: these do not belong to chain stores, have a sales space of less
than 400 square meters and usually specialise in packaged groceries. Food accounts
for at least 50% of total retail sales. Sometimes, independent grocers specialise in one
type of product, e.g., meat.
f. Free-standing food specialist: such as butchers and bakers are often independent
and are usually considered traditional retailers. Often, these retailers operate on open
markets or have free-standing retail sales points.
128. While the above terminology applies to most countries, in Malta, the channels through which
the grocery retail industry reaches its customers are more limited, and distinctions are more
obscured to a certain extent.
129. In line with previous assessments and decisions published by the Office for Competition
concerning the grocery retail sector, the Office distinguishes between five types of stores in
Malta: supermarkets, discounters, convenience stores, independent grocers, and free-
standing food specialists. Each type of store could be further subdivided between in-store and
online delivered groceries.

sales floor area, the range of products available, the prices charged, the quality of the
products, and the service offered.38

133. This categorisation is important because the different store types cater to different consumer
needs. For example, convenience stores are often located near residential areas, offering off-
street parking and/or convenient pedestrian access. Convenience stores are relatively small
outlets that are open long hours, and consumers use them mainly for “fill-in” purchases, such
as bread, milk, or miscellaneous goods. Such stores usually carry a rather limited line of high-
turnover convenience products but at high prices. On the contrary, supermarkets and
discounters are usually located on the village outskirts, operate in high volume, and its

produce, dairy products, baked goods) and household sundries. The distinction between
supermarkets and discount stores has become blurred, but discount stores tend to appeal
more to price-sensitive consumers. Given the small size of Malta, the distinction between
supermarkets and discounters is even more vague. Indeed, while the majority of product
categories, the 78 grocery retail outlets that responded to a RFI question to the Office
confirmed that they do perceive brands sold by Lidl outlets in Malta as a perfect substitute to
the corresponding products they sell, the PQRS analysis finds that Lidl competes across all
categories, not only on price but also on product range (cf. Table 4).39 Online grocery stores
cater for the most time-conscious and less mobile consumers.

5. RELEVANT MARKET
150. Market definition provides a framework for assessing the competitive effects of a
concentration and involves an element of judgement. The boundaries of the market are in
themselves an analytical tool – a means to an end – and do not determine the outcome of the
analysis of the competitive effects of the concentration. There could be external factors to the
relevant market that could exert constraint on the subject parties. Defining relevant markets
is a systematic methodology adopted by the Office for Competition for highlighting immediate
competitive constraints faced by the parties involved in the concentration.
151. Regulation 2 of the Control of Concentrations Regulations defines the relevant market as
”…the market for the products or services whether within Malta or
limited to any particular area or locality within Malta or outside Malta,
and whether or not restricted to a particular period of time or season
of the year”.
152. Market definition typically contains two dimensions: the product and geographic markets. As
stated in the European Commission’s notice on the definition of the relevant market
(C/2024/1645),
“The main purpose of market definition is to identify in a systematic
way the effective and immediate competitive constraints faced by
the undertakings involved when they offer particular products in a
particular area. Market definition leads to the identification of the
relevant competitors of the undertaking(s) involved when they offer
those products, as well as the relevant customers. Only products
that exert effective and immediate competitive constraints within the
relevant timeframe form part of the same relevant market as those
Office for Competition - 34 -

of the undertaking(s) involved, while other less effective, or merely
potential, constraints are considered as part of the competitive
assessment.”. 50
153. For the purposes of this decision, the Office for Competition retained the same methodology
adopted in the assessment of the previous concentrations involving the same Parties. The
methodology adopted in this decision shall not be construed as the starting point on which
future assessments will develop.
5.1. Product Market
154. This section defines the appropriate definition of the product market for the purpose of
providing the framework for the competitive assessment of the proposed concentration.
155. The relevant product market concept implies that there can be effective competition between
the products that form part of it. In the European Commission’s notice on market definition, it
is stated that “The relevant product market comprises all those products that customers regard
as interchangeable or substitutable to the product(s) of the undertaking(s) involved, based on
the products’ characteristics, their prices and their intended use, taking into consideration the
conditions of competition and the structure of supply and demand on the market”.51
156. In considering the relevant product market for this assessment, the Office has drawn on the
analysis undertaken in the groceries market investigation, and, where relevant, has presented
that analysis in this section and in Appendix B.
157. When defining the relevant product market, the Office has taken into account factors related
to both demand and supply.
5.1.1. Retail Grocery Market
158. When it comes to purchasing groceries, consumers can choose between a wide range of
stores. From a consumer’s perspective, there are a number of factors that set different stores
apart. These factors include characteristics like Price, Range of products, Quality of products,
and Services, such as parking availability and opening hours.52 All of these factors together
make up what we call the “retail offer”, or in other words, what the store is offering to
consumers. Some of these factors, like price and range of product, can be varied by retailers
relatively easily and quickly, while other factors, such as parking facilities and store layout,
are less easily or quickly changed.
159. In line with previous decisions, the Office considers that store size captures many aspects of
the retail offer of any given store. As a result, in line with previous decisions, the Office
analyses and describes the relevant product market in terms of store size. The Office has
previously established the definitions for different types of retail stores. ‘Supermarkets and
discount stores’ are self-service grocery stores with a sales floor area exceeding 200 square
meters and offering a wider range of products relative to the other retail trade channels.
‘Grocery and convenience stores’ and independent food specialists’ are retail outlets with a
sales floor area of less than 200 square meters, which sell a variety of grocery products.
Certain convenience stores are owned by companies that have a chain of convenience stores

173. The Office emphasises that the reason behind this delineation by store size is that from a
demand-side perspective, small stores are not considered to be good substitutes for larger
stores on the basis that they may not supply the full range of products which a larger store
offers and therefore, may not be able to cater for groceries that involve larger or wider range
of products. In fact, it is typically concluded that the competitive constraints faced by grocery
stores is asymmetric in the sense that large stores do impose competitive constraints on
smaller stores but not vice-versa.
174. Based on the PQRS, set out in Section 5.1.2 and in more detail in Appendix B, the Office
analysed the extent of the competitive constraint imposed on the Notifying Party. Each store
was classified as either being within the relevant product market or outside the relevant
product market. The classification based on the PQRS analysis was then considered against
several headline indicators (such as turnover, expenditure spent per customer, the
percentage of sales accounted for food items, identification of competitors, etc.) to ensure that
the definition of the relevant product market is based on sensible criteria. This detailed
assessment of the headline indicators, together with further analysis of the data gathered from
the RFI to the grocery retail outlets, can be found in Appendix B of this Report.
175. In line with its previous decisions, the Office notes that there is a strong correlation between
store size and product range for stores with sales area larger than 200 square metres, with a
correlation coefficient of more than 0.8. This means that in relation to product range, larger
stores typically carry a larger number of different products than smaller stores. To the extent
that products are available in larger stores but not in smaller stores, this will affect the extent
to which consumers view shopping in a smaller store as a satisfactory substitute for shopping
in a larger store. Indeed, this relationship between store size and product range supports the
view that customers may not find stores with less floorspace an effective substitute for stores
with more floorspace due to their smaller range of products.
176. The size of a store can offer different types of amenities to customers, such as parking
availability and loyalty schemes. This can influence whether customers view these stores as
substitutes for one another. Generally, larger stores are more likely to offer a greater range of
other amenities, which distinguishes them from smaller stores. The Office has found that the
availability of a range of amenities increases with store size.

Amalgamation of Stores
202. The Notifying Party believes that the affected product market should be re-assessed and
should include, organised grocery retail networks with an aggregate floor space equal to or in
excess of 200 square meters. This is because a number of convenience shop outlets in the
relevant geographic market, may be compared in sales floor area to 2 or 3 medium-sized
supermarkets in excess of 200 square meters when taken together. Therefore, according to
the Notifying Party, the consequent exclusion of a number of undertakings from the relevant
product market on this basis, should be reviewed and/ or reconsidered, given that such
approach is likely to lead to a skewed delineation of the market realities currently at play in
the Maltese grocery sector.
203. The Office asserts that the amalgamation of sales floor areas of nearby stores should be
avoided, and the competitive assessment is to be based on each store, even those that are
in the same operator’s chain. This method is grounded in several factors, as explained further
below.
204. To begin, when assessing the potential competition effects and determining the presence of
competitive constraints, the approach involves differentiating between store sizes. Therefore,
the aggregation of these stores, as suggested by the Notifying Party, would essentially blur
the distinctions in store sizes. This approach risks categorising any mini-market, grocer, or
discount chain as a supermarket or hypermarket, irrespective of their pricing strategy, even if
they constitute part of the same small-stores chain. It is important to recognise that the store
size principal, as demonstrated by the PQRS analysis provided in Section 5.1.2 and in more
detail in Appendix B, is an important aspect in the evaluation of competition within the retail
market, in particular because of product range. Treating stores within the same town or
geographical area as a one store not only alters why chains choose to cluster stores in
88 J Sainsbury PLC / Asda Group Ltd merger inquiry, decision of CMA, dated 25 April 2019.
Office for Competition - 45 -

particular areas but also overlooks why smaller stores have different price, quality, range and
service strategies and their presence in strategic locations.
205. Additionally, amalgamation of small stores would also overlook the fact that typically it is sales-
per-square foot, not local community need, that dictate where supermarket chains choose to
locate. For example, when a convenience store or supermarket chooses to open a new outlet
first sift locations according a wide range of factors – population density, footfall, the proximity
of certain locations such as shopping malls, business centres, hotels and entertainment hubs
nearby, schools or attractions, amongst others.89 Furthermore, smaller stores are subject to
competitive constrains from other convenience and smaller stores due to relatively the same
revenue base.
206. Moreover, the European Commission and competition authorities rely their assessment on
stores/points of sale to evaluate proposed concentrations, specifically focusing on distinct
types such as hypermarkets, supermarkets, minimarkets, and discount stores.90 Competition
authorities have used analysis of catchment areas to identify areas where the Parties’ stores
overlap. Stores are likely to be alternatives for some customers, and therefore competitors, if
their catchment areas overlap. If the Parties’ catchment areas overlap, then further analysis
will be required to determine whether a substantive competition lessening may arise.
207. Furthermore, each of these points of sale is meticulously differentiated based on various
characteristics like size, positioning, product range, presence of fresh food counters, and other
factors that contribute to determining their quality and level of services. Also, a large one-stop
shop grocery store typically has a 10- to 15-minute catchment area, whereas a small grocery
store has a much smaller catchment area.91 So, aggregating smaller stores into one would
also distort the geographic market catchment area to discussed further in the next section.
208. From a supply perspective, smaller outlets cannot take advantage of economies of scale. This
implies that their average cost per unit remains high or decreases less significantly as they
expand their operations by opening further small outlets. Smaller stores belonging to the same
chain can benefit from certain economies of scale due centralised purchasing, streamlined
logistics, and shared marketing efforts. However, the extent of these benefits may not match
those of supermarket chains due to differences in scale. For example, certain costs
associated with operating a grocery business, such as rent, utilities, and staffing, are
essentially fixed or have significant indivisible components that remain constant regardless of
the size of the store. Utilities and staffing costs may not scale linearly with store size, meaning
that the larger supermarket can spread these fixed costs more thinly per unit of sales
compared to the smaller convenience stores. Therefore, while both the supermarket and
convenience stores chains benefit from economies of scale to some extent, the indivisibility
of certain costs allows the supermarket to realise greater cost efficiencies. Therefore,
aggregating outlets would distort the supply-side characteristics of each store and the fact
that they each have different points of sale.
209. Moreover, aggregating multiple small stores of identical chain affiliation within the product
market would defy rationale due to the implication that consumers exhibit indifference
between purchasing from distinct localities within the same chain network. Such an
interpretation would suggest that consumers regard the geographical distinction between
stores as unimportant to their purchasing decisions, or that their selection of one small store
over another is based solely on the presence of another proximate small-scale outlet under
the same chain umbrella. Consequently, this argument would posit these smaller outlets as

5.1.2. PQRS Analysis
211. The classification of stores with a sales area of 200 square metres or more, as either being
within or outside the relevant product market, is based on the PQRS analysis undertaken by
the Office. This involved a review of the characteristics of stores that might lie in the same
relevant product market to gauge customers’ willingness to switch between stores in the event
of changes in the relative prices.
212. The Office also considered characteristics other than price because customers typically
choose between alternative stores by weighting the various store characteristics, such as
quality, range and service including parking facilities and loyalty schemes amongst others.
Each customer implicitly ranks the various differentiated alternatives according to the extent
to which each store’s overall combination of attributes and characteristics meets his or her
preferences.
213. The relevance of the characteristics for the definition of the relevant product market are
supported by the replies from a demand-side survey conducted by the Office in 202092 which
revealed that the PQRS characteristics are highly relevant for customers’ store choice
decisions. Specifically in this survey, 76.4% of respondents considered ‘low prices’ as very
important when choosing a store for their main grocery shopping, while 63.8% of respondents
considered as very important the availability of branded products.
214. Similarly, respondents considered several factors as being important in relation to the quality
and service offered by grocery stores, namely freshness and variety of fruit and vegetables
(86%), quality and variety of delicatessen (88%) and meat freshness (82%) in case of quality
and customer service (89.4%), parking area (83.5%), opening on Sunday (75.9%) and special
offers and deals (71.7%) in the case of service. Moreover, 83.5% of respondents consider
location as very important when choosing their grocery outlet.

Price
216. The rationale for the classification of stores based on ‘price’ is that any product price which is
approximately equal to the mean price charged by a selected group of supermarkets
(henceforth the ‘select group’) imposes some competitive constraint. The classification is
based on an analysis that benchmarks stores’ prices with those of the select group that are
easily identifiable as direct competitors to each other. These include the stores belonging to
the Notifying Party (“Lidl” outlets), the stores belonging to the Target (“Scotts” outlets), Smart
Supermarket Ltd., PG Group (namely, PAVI supermarket and PAMA supermarket), Greens
supermarkets and Welbee’s supermarkets (owned by Retail Marketing Limited).
217. The ‘select group’ were chosen by first analysing the results of the RFI responses on product
substitutability presented in Appendix B. Most of the grocery retail outlets that the Office is
considering under the ‘select group’, have stated that they consider their product categories
to be substitutable to the brands on offer by Lidl outlets, thus emphasizing the fact that for the
‘select group’, Lidl is considered to be in direct competition in the market and thus imposing a
competitive constraint on the ‘select group’. Moreover, the ‘select group’ are the most
important market players in the grocery retail sector.
218. The Office deemed stores to impose a competitive constraint on the Notifying Party if at least
40% of their products are within one standard deviation of the average price of the select
group of supermarkets. A detailed explanation of the pricing analysis is provided in Appendix
B.
219. The results of the pricing analysis are summarised in Appendix B. A ‘Yes’ entry in the ‘Price’
column indicates that at least 40% of the products sold by the store are within one standard
deviation of the average price of the select group of supermarkets. Overall, fifty-three out of
the eighty-seven stores that have a sales area equal to or more than 200 square meters, are
deemed to have imposed some competitive constraint on the Notifying Party through their
pricing.
Quality
220. For the quality assessment the Office does not produce a store classification analysis. The
reason is that the eighty-seven stores that have a sales area of 200 square meters or more
typically sell products with similar brands. This means that the products sold by most stores
are generally regarded by customers as being of good and/or similar quality.
221. A notable exception is Lidl which only sells a few products with similar brands to those sold
by other grocery retailers. Nonetheless, in a demand-side survey conducted by the Office in
202093 showed that 93% of Lidl’s customers either ‘strongly agree’ or ‘agree’ that Lidl’s
products are of good quality, even though their brands are not well known. Most of the product
categories were highly rated for their quality by customers, namely, refrigerated products, food
cupboard items, beverages, pet food, health and beauty products.
222. The Office notes that having good quality products is an important factor for customers when
choosing their main grocery retail outlet for shopping. Thus, supermarkets need to maintain
the quality of their products at a high standard to be able to compete for customers with each
other.

224. The rationale for the classification of stores based on ‘range’ is that any store that belongs to
the same relevant market as that of the Notifying Party must offer a range of products that is
similar to that offered by the stores owned by the Notifying Party. Specifically, stores are
deemed to impose a competitive constraint on the Notifying Party if their range of products
within product groupings (e.g., oil, pasta, fresh vegetables, fresh meat, beer and ciders, etc.)
is at least as much as that offered by the minimum of the Notifying Party’s stores in at least
50% of these product groupings. A detailed explanation of the product range analysis is
provided in Appendix B.

‘Range’ column indicates that at least 50% of the range of products within product groupings
is at least as much as that offered by the minimum of the Notifying Party’s stores. Overall,
forty-six out of the eighty-seven stores that have a sales area of 200 square meters or more
imposed some competitive constraint on the Notifying Party through the range of their
products.
Service
226. Consumers typically consider the level of service (e.g. customer service, parking facilities,
opening on Sundays, etc.) offered by a grocery retail outlet. Hence, grocery stores that belong
to the same product market as the Notifying Party must offer at least some similar services.
Specifically, only stores that have at least four of a selection of eighty “good-service”
characteristics, were deemed to impose a competitive constraint on the Notifying Party. These
good customer service characteristics include opening on Sundays, parking facilities, toilet
facilities, online shopping, customer support desks, loyalty schemes, discounts and whether
stores form part of a shopping mall. A detailed explanation of the service analysis is provided
in Appendix B.
227. The results of the customer service analysis are summarised in Appendix B. A ‘Yes’ entry in
the ‘Service’ column indicates that the store has four or more good service characteristics
from those listed above. Overall, fifty-two out of eighty-seven stores that have a sales area of
200 square meters or more are deemed to have imposed some competitive constraint on the
Notifying Party through their service.

5.2. Geographic Market
243. The European Commission defines the relevant geographic market as
“comprises the geographic area in which the undertakings involved
supply or demand relevant products, in which the conditions of
competition are sufficiently homogeneous for the effects of the
conduct or concentration under investigation to be able to be
assessed, and which can be distinguished from other geographic
areas, in particular because conditions of competition are
appreciably different in those areas”.102
244. When defining the geographic market for concentrations in the grocery retail sector, European
case law generally distinguishes between national and local aspects to competition.103
245. According to the Notifying Party’s submissions, the parties to the concentration consider the
relevant national geographic market to be Malta. The Office for Competition concurs with the
Notifying Party’s views in the sense that the geographic market definition should exclude retail
grocery stores situated and operating in the island of Gozo. This is because of an additional
travel time of around 20 minutes (the average time taken by a typical ferry crossing between
the two islands’ closest geographic points) and related ferry expenses.
246. To delineate the local geographic market, the Office refers to the methodology proposed in
the Merger Assessment Guidelines issued by the Competition Commission and the Office of
Fair Trading whereby it is stated that:
“When assessing mergers involving a large number of local
geographic markets – for example, mergers of grocery retailers
operating over multiple localities – the Authorities may examine the
geographic catchment area within which the great majority of a
store’s custom is located. Catchment areas are a pragmatic
approximation for a candidate market to which the hypothetical
monopolist test can be applied; the use of catchment areas is not an
alternative conceptual approach. However, the geographic market
is identified using the hypothetical monopolist test will typically be
wider than a catchment area, Consequently, if the impact of the
merger on concentration in this catchment area appears
unproblematic, then the Authorities may exclude the local area from
further analysis without concluding on the boundaries of that
particular relevant geographic market”. 104
247. The Parties contend that the geographic market should include, organised grocery retail
networks with an aggregate floor space equal to or in excess of 200 square meters in the

retail sale of daily consumer goods is local in nature, the exact geographical scope
corresponding to a catchment area around each store, based on travel distance to the store.
In previous decisions, the Commission has considered a zone of 10, 20, or 30 minutes of

more than 2,500 square meter, have a larger catchment area (20 to 30 minutes) than smaller

attracting new customers without significantly impacting the existing customer base of the
older store.
260. For opening a new store to be commercially viable it has to either be without cannibalisation
or minimised cannibalisation, meaning that that the supermarket chain is successfully
expanding its reach without sacrificing the performance of its existing stores. Because the
population density and socio-economic conditions in Zabbar and nearby localities such as in
Zejtun and Luqa is more or less the same, the schedule of distances between each of Lidl
outlets and the nearest store of the store to be acquired is indicative of the initial catchment
distance. Assuming that each Lidl store serves more or less a distinct local area, it is likely
that with similar footfall and economic conditions, the location where Scotts in Zabbar is
located has a strategic positioning such that it minimises overlap and cannibalisation. This
suggests for Scotts in Zabbar to be commercially viable the initial catchment area is about 11
minutes away.
5.2.2. Willingness to Travel
261. The Office typically calculates an average catchment area for a sample of stores, like in Retail
Marketing Limited. However, in this case, given the nature of the proposed transaction, the
Office has calculated the catchment area for the individual store through an exit-store survey.
Office for Competition - 58 -

The individual store catchment areas can be informative where people living in different places
are willing to travel very different distances to visit a store, and where differences in travel
patterns are not related to observable factors such as whether the area is in an urban or rural
area. However, catchment areas for an individual store depend on the number of stores in the
local area – customers do not need to commute far if there are lots of stores in the local area.
Since store catchment areas are not solely related to customers’ willingness to travel, it is
deemed preferable to complement results from the exit-store surveys with other methods.

travel time individuals are willing to commit to reach a supermarket or grocery store is 15

range of products offered, with 35% of responses, indicating that customers value variety and
selection when choosing where to shop. Additionally, 18% of respondents cited service and

as a key factor that influences their decision.111

5.2.5. Catchment Area (Loyalty Card Data)
Office for Competition - 63 -

273. The loyalty card data is an alternative data source used to identify the geographic market. It
focuses on the behaviour of “loyal” customers and can also define catchment areas. These
areas, based on loyalty card data, are likely narrower than the overall geographic market.
However, they help the Office confirm its estimates of the relevant geographic market using
exit-store surveys. While not all customers utilise loyalty cards for their grocery purchases,
particularly for spontaneous purchases, these cards play an important role in modern
marketing strategies that prioritise rewarding customer loyalty, offering exclusive discounts,
freebies, and prizes on their shopping. As the marketing landscape has evolved, there has
been a shift towards incentivising and acknowledging loyal customers who accumulate points
through their purchases. Consequently, loyalty cards have become essential tools for
supermarkets to foster and retain customer loyalty by offering incentives, thereby increasing
the likelihood of customers sticking with one brand. However, when many people hold multiple
loyalty cards, nearby stores with competing offers might cancel each other out, resulting in
more imitation than innovation.112
274. There are valid justifications for using both driving-time isochrones (based on consumer
surveys) and catchment areas (derived from loyalty card data) from a conceptual standpoint.
Defining markets based on driving time radii, for example, requires less extensive and high-
quality data. Conversely, employing actual catchment areas provides the benefit of being
directly rooted in the actual purchasing behaviours of customers, thereby implicitly
encompassing the unique circumstances surrounding each individual location (such as the
presence of competitors and other stores, topographical features, and traffic).
275. Competition Authorities have used catchment areas covering a certain percentage (usually
over 60%) of a store’s sales or customers. There is no set rule, and this decision is typically
made to complement customer surveys. By way of example,
a. in the Pure Gym/The Gym case (2014), the CMA found that competition was assessed
within a narrower area than the usual 80% catchment. Instead, they carefully examined
each overlapping area, moving away from a catchment area-focused approach.
b. in the Greene King/Spirit Pub case (2015), the CMA employed 60% catchment areas
because customers living closer to the pub tended to visit more frequently, contributing
a larger share of revenue.
c. in the Tesco plc/The Co-operative Group case (2007), the Competition Commission
used Tesco Clubcard data to determine where sales originated and used that
information to identify the store's competition constraints.
d. in the Kaufland Stiftung & Co. KG/SCP Retail Operations S.à r.l. case (2020), the
Bundeskartellamt used the actual catchment areas of the target locations based on
geographically differentiated turnover data.113

strengthens the validity, giving confidence in the conclusions drawn from the assessment of
the geographic market.

292. Based on the above analysis, taking into consideration, the topography of Zabbar, customers'
