6. THEORETICAL OVERVIEW: ASSESSMENT OF COMPETITIVE EFFECTS
293. This section gives an overview of the theories of harm considered, the general approach for
assessing them, evaluates the interrelations between the Parties' activities, and provide an
overview of the information and evidence gathered.
6.1. Outline of the Theories of Harm
294. Theories of harm serve as a framework for evaluating the impact of a concentration. Such
theories articulate potential scenarios in which changes to the market structure could
empower the merged entity to wield market influence, resulting in a substantial lessening of
competition. In essence, a theory of harm explains behaviour that harms competition, violating
competition law and warranting prohibition. Additionally, it delineates potential shifts resulting
from the concentration, comparing the effects on competition and anticipated harm to
consumers with the pre-concentration scenario.
Office for Competition - 68 -

295. The following theories of harm have been identified related to the specific market and can be
grouped in two areas:
a. Retail groceries (in-store and online)
i. Horizontal unilateral effects at both the national and the local level
ii. Coordinated effects
b. Buyer power theories of harm, including both the effect on innovation and the effect on
rivals’ purchasing costs (the ‘waterbed effect’)
296. These theories of harm explore how the horizontal overlap between the activities of the
Parties, operating within the same industry and supply chain level, could significantly reduce
competition (substantial lessening of competition) in their respective markets post-
concentration. The theories of harm illustrate how consumer harm might arise after the
concentration, including increased prices for consumers and potential negative impacts on
quality, innovation, or consumer choice.
297. Our approach to analysing harm theories involves assessing how concentration may impact
the Parties' ability to raise prices or compromise non-price aspects of their offerings, such as
quality, variety, or service (referred to as ‘PQRS’). We compare this assessment to a scenario
without concentration. When we use the term ‘deteriorating’, we mean that in the absence of
concentration, the Parties would likely still improve certain aspects of PQRS due to existing
market competition. However, if concentration occurs and competition significantly
diminishes, the Parties are less incentivised to enhance both price and non-price factors. As
a result, concentration could lead to a decline in market conditions compared to what would
have naturally occurred.
298. In our assessment, we investigate whether this decline would affect aspects of PQRS that are
standardized across all of the Parties’ stores, impacting their national operations, or if it would
only impact elements that vary across local areas, affecting specific stores within the Parties’
network (local assessment).
6.2. Approach to Assessing Theories of Harm
6.2.1. Horizontal Unilateral Effects Theories of Harm
299. Horizontal unilateral effects are likely to arise when a concentration between two competing
firms eliminates a rival in the market, thus eliminating the competitive constraint previously
provided by a competitor. As a result, the acquirer has the ability to profitably increase prices,
lower quality, reduce the range of their services and/or reduce innovation (relative to the
situation that would have existed absent the concentration). This occurs the detriment of
consumers despite the responses of the remaining competitors present in the market. Such
phenomenon takes place even if the firm’s remaining rivals do not change their conduct, as it
is now less costly for the acquirer to increase its prices. Furthermore, the acquirer has the
ability to create barriers to entry or expansion of competitors.
300. Under such theories, the harm occurs since the proposed acquisition acts unilaterally,
independently of other players in the market. Furthermore, competitors of the acquirer may
also, unilaterally, increase their prices or worsen their offering (“second order effects”) which
may lead to further consumer harm.
301. These horizontal theories of harm are assessed by determining how significant a competitor
of one of the concentration parties is to the other, or is likely to become in the foreseeable
future, relative to other competitive constraints in the market; and whether the removal of that
Office for Competition - 69 -

constraint is likely to lead to a substantial lessening of competition, and thus undesirable
outcomes for consumers.
302. Market shares are not the only determining factors to assess whether a concentration will give
rise to unilateral effects. Other factors are also considered, such as the ease with which rival
firms can expand their output and the dynamic responses that those rivals might make in
response to attempts by the acquirer to increase price. Thus, examining competitive
assessment in the market goes typically goes beyond a simple static analysis (based primarily
on market shares) but on one that explicitly adopts a dynamic assessment (that considers the
scope for a firm to expand output and/or reposition their respective product offerings, including
the introduction of new products).
6.2.2. Coordinated Effects Theories of Harm
303. Coordinated effects refers to the possibility that after the concentration takes place, the firms
involved in the concentration (at least an important subset of) and their rivals will increase
their market power by coordinating their actions, as they realise that they are mutually
interdependent.
304. Coordinated effects arise when a concentration makes coordination more likely or more
effective. This behaviour does not require any direct contact between firms and can arise
purely from firms’ perception of the interdependence between them. Coordination can be
explicit or tacit. The focus is on whether the concentration could make it easier for market
players to coordinate or align their behaviour in a way which limits the rivalry between them
without entering into any express agreement or direct communication.
305. Any theory of harm based on coordinated effects must explain in what ways firms in the
coordinating group moderate their competitive behaviour so as to achieve higher prices. Such
moderating behaviour can take a number of forms, including directly raising prices, limiting
production or limiting the amount of new capacity brought into the market.
6.2.3. Buyer Power Theory of Harm
306. Buyer Power theory of harm refers to the possibility that where the Parties to the concentration
purchase the same products, they will now have greater buyer power than they could have
previously exerted individually.
307. It refers to buyers' ability to act to alter the supply market’s structure. The presence of buyer
power may serve to counter the exercise of pricing power by suppliers, and thereby mitigate
unilateral price rises that may otherwise occur following a concentration.
308. For the purposes of competitive assessments, concerns arise only if an increase in the buyer
power of the acquirer distorts competition in relation to the supply of groceries and thus results
in adverse effects on end-consumers. In and of itself, a reduction in the profitability of suppliers
does not give rise to a substantial lessening of competition.
309. In such concentrations, there are two theories of harm which are usually considered in this
aspect:
a. the exercise of increased buyer power by the Notifying Parties might result in reduced
incentives to invest and innovate on the part of suppliers; and
b. the exercise of increased buyer power by the Notifying Parties might raise the
purchasing costs of rival grocery retailers, which, under certain circumstances, may
result in price increases to certain end-customers of those retailers.

6.2.4. GUPPI Methodology
310. This section outlines the method and strategy used for deriving Gross Upward Pricing
Pressure Index (hereinafter referred to as “GUPPI”) based on the outcomes of the exit-store
survey which the Office for Competition commissioned. The diversion ratios will be combined
with information on the Parties’ variable profit margins and the ratio of the Parties’ prices to
estimate GUPPI.
311. The GUPPI test, also known as the upward price pressure test, is a tool developed by
economists in recent years to offer a measurable indication of an undertaking inclination to
raise prices or worsen the PQRS post-concentration.
312. The GUPPI considers two crucial factors influencing the inclination of the firms that are parties
to the concentration to increase prices or deter the product offer after a concentration:
a. the Acquirer’s profit margin on the product it sells; and
b. the diversion ratio of its customers to the Acquirer
313. The GUPPI offers advantages when it is difficult to clearly define the product market,
especially in markets with differentiated products. Consequently, the GUPPI serves as a
valuable tool for evaluating competition intensity in such scenarios. As a result, the Office
considers the GUPPI as a supplementary tool to assess the likelihood of exacerbating any or
all competitive parameters for either of the Parties, thereby indicating a concentration effect.

317. The GUPPI formula highlights the following principles:
i. A higher diversion ratio corresponds to a higher GUPPI, indicating that products of the
concentration firms serve as close substitutes. Consequently, the other party to the
concentration recaptures more lost sales when raising prices post-concentration.
ii. A higher profit margin leads to a higher GUPPI, reflecting the profitability of the products
offered for sale. This margin is typically calculated as the difference between the price
and the variable contribution margin, acting as a proxy for actual costs incurred.
Office for Competition - 71 -

iii. A higher price ratio results in a higher GUPPI, converting diverted value from euros to
percentages for easier comparison across concentrations.
318. The fundamental principle underlying the GUPPI is that post-concentration, one of the parties
involved may find it economically advantageous to degrade its offerings, as it can recuperate
profits from customers who transition from the products of the other party.
319. In practical terms, for Lidl, its GUPPI can be calculated as the multiplication of three factors:
a. the diversion ratio from Scotts to Lidl,
b. Lidl’s variable profit margin, and
c. the price ratio between the two parties.
320. The diversion ratio represents the percentage of Scotts’s customers, that currently do not
shop at Lidl, who would have chosen to make their purchases at Lidl, if Scotts Zabbar was
transferred to a Lidl outlet. The variable profit margin is the difference between the additional
sales revenue and the incremental cost incurred to generate that revenue. If there are price
discrepancies between the two parties, the GUPPI would also need adjustment based on the
corresponding price ratio.

7. COMPETITIVE ASSESSMENT
323. The competitive assessment is based on the turnover figures provided by the Parties and third
parties, with data collected by December 2023 through a RFI issued on 23rd November 2023.
7.1. Impact of Concentration on Market Structure
324. In the context of an acquisition, unilateral effects refer to situations where an acquiring
undertaking acquires a competitor, enabling the acquirer to potentially increase its market
share and then be able to raise prices or degrade non-price aspects of its competitive offering
(such as quality, range, service and innovation) on its own and without needing to coordinate
with its rivals. These effects can affect customers across different levels of the supply chain
and are not limited to end consumers. The acquisition may eliminate a competitive constraint,
whether existing or potential, thereby altering the competitive dynamics of the market.
325. Evaluating the acquisition, the main concern lies in assessing whether there will be sufficient
remaining alternatives for customers post-concentration to constrain the acquirer’s market
power. Factors such as market concentration and barriers to entry or expansion are crucial
considerations in this assessment. Measures of concentration, including market shares,
number of competitors, and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), are utilised to analyse the
competitive landscape and potential anti-competitive effects of the acquisition.
326. The HHI is a measure of market concentration that takes account of the differences in the
sizes of market participants, as well as their number. The HHI is calculated by adding together
the squared values of the percentage market shares of all firms in the market.122 The change
in the HHI (known as the ‘delta’) can be calculated by subtracting the market’s pre-
concentration HHI from its expected post-concentration HHI.
327. The post-concentration HHI gives an indication of the level of market concentration while the
change in the HHI (or ‘delta’) reflects the change in market concentration resulting from the
acquisition. Together, the post-concentration level and the change in the HHI are used to form
a threshold of market concentration. The Commission will have regard to the following
thresholds:
a. A post-concentration HHI below 1,000 is unlikely to cause concern.
b. Any market with a post-concentration HHI greater than 1,000 may be regarded as
concentrated and highly concentrated if greater than 2,000.
c. Except as noted below, in a concentrated market a delta of less than 250 is unlikely to
cause concern and in a highly concentrated market a delta of less than 150 is unlikely
to cause concern.
328. However, a concentration that falls below the HHI thresholds may still raise competition
concerns in certain circumstances such as, for example, where one of the parties to the
concentration has a dominant position. Indeed, according to the Guidelines on the
assessment of horizontal mergers under the Council Regulation on the control of
concentrations between undertakings:
“According to well-established case law, very large market shares
— 50% or more — may in themselves be evidence of the existence

geographic markets – for example, mergers of grocery retailers
operating over multiple localities – the Authorities may examine the
geographic catchment area within which the great majority of a
store’s custom is located. Catchment areas are a pragmatic
approximation for a candidate market to which the hypothetical

unproblematic, then the Authorities may exclude the local area from

353. The term ‘counterfactual’ refers to the state of competition without the acquisition. In other
words, the “actual” situation is the acquisition being put into effect and the “counterfactual” is
Office for Competition - 84 -

the situation in the absence of the acquisition being put into effect. The counterfactual
provides the reference point, or the point of comparison, for assessing competitive effects
arising from an acquisition.
354. Based on the collected evidence, the Office concluded that the counterfactual in this case
should be the prevailing market conditions of competition, and including the new Eurospin
stores in Mosta and Marsa, Welbee’s at the Shoreline Mall in Smart City, and the new Lidl
store outlet in Zebbug. The Office is also aware that Scotts closed its Santa Lucija operation
on 6th May 2024.129 For this reason, the exit from Santa Lucija is considered to be part of the
counterfactual, as explained in paragraphs 98-102. []
355. As Eurospin and Lidl are the only two discounters operating in Malta, the Office assumes that
the projected turnover generated by Eurospin will be cannibalised from Lidl’s market share.
This extreme scenario is adopted to illustrate the potential extent of a substantial lessening of
competition, even in this highly competitive environment. In reality, Eurospin’s entry into the
market is expected to affect not only Lidl but also other supermarkets and grocery retailers.
While it is true that Lidl and Eurospin are the only two discounters in Malta, the competitive
dynamics extend beyond just these two players. Eurospin’s competitive pricing and offerings
are likely to attract customers from a variety of supermarkets, including both discount and
supermarkets. Therefore, in a more realistic scenario, Eurospin’s entry would lead to a
redistribution of turnover among multiple competitors, rather than solely cannibalising Lidl’s
market share.
356. The turnover of Lidl generated from Eurospin in Marsa is assumed to be conditional on the
driving distance between the two stores. Specifically, the premise is that the likelihood of
Eurospin drawing turnover from a particular Lidl store decreases as the distance between
them increases. In other words, Lidl stores located farther away from Eurospin are perceived
to be less susceptible to losing turnover to Eurospin due to reduced convenience for
customers.
357. The Office has requested Lidl, via a RFI, to provide the projected revenues for all its existing
stores, including the Zabbar store in the event of Lidl acquiring it. Lidl conducted an analysis
to estimate the cannibalisation effect on its revenues, which involved assessing the potential
impact of the newly acquired stores on the turnover of existing Lidl stores, particularly those
in close proximity. The Office has integrated these projected revenues into its assessment to
comprehensively evaluate the competitive implications of the acquisition. By considering the
effects of cannibalisation, the Office aims to grasp how the addition of the Zabbar store and
to Lidl’s portfolio and the new Zebbug store might influence market dynamics and competition
within the grocery retail sector.
358. Given that several stores either opened in 2023 or are scheduled to open after 2023, and
some partially opened in 2022, the Office has utilised projected or annualised revenue figures
to account for a full year’s operation. This approach ensures that the assessment reflects the
scenario where stores are fully operational, thereby capturing the long-term competitive
effects. Additionally, to facilitate comparison across multiple years, the Office has adjusted
the revenue figures to 2022 prices using the Retail Price Index (RPI) and forecasted RPI data
from the Central Bank of Malta. This adjustment to 2022 prices ensures consistency and
enables meaningful comparisons of revenue figures over time, allowing for a comprehensive
analysis of market dynamics and competitive effects.

Council Regulation on the control of concentrations between undertakings.

405. In the context of assessing an acquisition in a local geographic market, it is essential to
evaluate whether the transaction would create SLC. The mere possibility of market entry by
potential competitors, irrespective the concentration, is not sufficient to rule out SLC. Instead,
there must be a clear and actual likelihood of market entry, supported by sufficient incentives
for new competitors to enter the market. This assessment focuses on whether market entry
would be likely, timely, and substantial enough to constrain the behaviour of the incumbent
Notifying Party. If the Notifying Party already holds a substantial market share position in the
market, even a small change in market conditions – such as the elimination of Scotts from the
local market – could strengthen this market position. In such cases, the removal of a potential
competitor might be enough to tip the balance towards, or at the very least reinforce, a
dominant market position. Therefore, when considering the post-acquisition market
conditions, the likelihood, timeliness, and sufficiency of potential market entry must be high to
justify approving the acquisition. Indeed, congruent with these principles, in Retail Marketing
Limited and Lidl/Scotts decision by the Office, did not include, inter alia, pending applications
with the Planning Authority.

applications do not meet the criteria for inclusion in the counterfactual scenario, the acquisition
of Scotts (Zabbar) must be assessed with this context in mind. Refer to section 3.3.1 and
Appendix E.

“In cases such as the present one, where the Bundeskartellamt

a concentration in the grocery sector is not an exceptional case. Indeed, effective remedies,
like divestitures or structural commitments, are standard and proven in this context.

446. The Office considers that there is uncertainty with the proposed ‘fix-it-later’ solution provided
by Lidl in its commitments. The level of competitive harm that would occur between the
completion of the concentration and the time Eurospin or any relevant competitor enters the
local market would persist for a significant time frame, potentially exceeding []. This duration
allows a substantial lessening of competition to remain in place far longer than is typical with
divestiture commitments, which generally remedy the issue within six months.
447. The Office is also of the view that there is no competitive rationale to keep the supermarket
closed for more than one year, when there could be the possibility for Scotts supermarket to
continue operating in this transitional period, or put to sale to other competitors, thus offering
an alternative for consumers. Moreover, consumers would be made worse-off if Scotts
supermarket would close-down and the premises vacated for the suggested time-period, as
there is one less competitor on the market, resulting in one less option for consumers to make
their shopping for a long period of time. If these commitments are accepted as they are, the
Office would also be precluding any other competitor from entering the market instead of
Scotts supermarket, that would have increased competition within the relevant geographic
market within the immediate to short-term. Furthermore, there are no certain guarantees that
a new entrant will enter the geographic market and solve the competitive issues imposed by
the large market shares that are currently occupied by Lidl.
448. The Office also recognises that behavioural commitments, such as the one proposed by Lidl,
often create uncertainty because they rely on future actions rather than immediate structural
changes. Unlike divestitures, which offer a clear and definitive remedy by removing overlaps
in competitive activities, behavioural remedies depend on the ongoing adherence to certain
conduct, which can be difficult to monitor and enforce. This uncertainty is exacerbated by the
potential delays and complications in ensuring compliance, leading to a prolonged period
during which competitive harm could persist. Therefore, the Office’s concerns are heightened
by the fact that this ‘fix-it-later’ approach will not adequately or promptly address the
competition issues at hand.
449. Therefore, the Office concludes that the Commitments of 24th May 2024 do not eliminate the
identified competition concerns entirely and are not comprehensive and effective from all
points of view. Furthermore, the Office is not able to conclude with the requisite degree of
certainty that it will be possible to implement them and that it is likely that the new commercial
structures resulting from them will be sufficiently workable and lasting to ensure that the
significant impediments to effective competition will not materialise.

9. CONCLUSIONS
450. The Office conducted a comprehensive competitive assessment, evaluating the degree of
competition between Lidl, Scotts, and other grocery retailers in both the current market
conditions (i.e., prevailing market conditions) and foreseeable future (i.e., counterfactual
scenario). The assessment incorporated a wide range of evidence to determine whether the
proposed acquisition might lead to SLC in the grocery retail market in both the national context
and the local geographic area.
451. On the basis of the prevailing market shares, the Notifying Party is the largest retailer in this
market at national level and has an even stronger position at local level. Scotts is a smaller
player in the market.
452. When considering the prevailing market conditions at the national level, Lidl is already a
market leader with a high market share, and such market shares would further increase if the
acquisition were approved. This heightened market power might provide the acquirer with the
ability and incentive to engage in anti-competitive behaviour, including foreclosing rivals from
the market, thereby impeding smaller competitors’ ability to compete effectively. Such actions
could ultimately diminish consumer welfare over the long term. Indeed, the parties’ responses
to RFIs underscore the limited availability of suitable locations for supermarkets, with Scotts
even claiming that [].155 Similarly, Lidl claims in the CN Form “the shortage in vacant
properties suitable for grocery outlets above 200sqm in sales floor area”, “the lack of available
properties for large supermarkets in the growing town [of Marsaskala]”, and “hefty increase in
price of immovable property across the board.” This implies that there is a likelihood of
unilateral anti-competitive behaviour by the acquirer should such concentration be realised
due to a higher concentrated market and higher barriers to entry or expand, albeit not
extensively at the national level.
453. When considering the counterfactual scenario, i.e., the scenario used to study the effect of
the proposed transaction, within a 15-minute driving time, Lidl’s market share is expected to
rise to []%. This would significantly strengthen Lidl’s local market position. The post-
acquisition HHI surpasses 2,000, with a delta of [400-450], indicating a marked increase in
market concentration and a higher likelihood of horizontal unilateral effects. This indicates
suggests a decline in competition, which could adversely affect price, quality, range, and
service (PQRS) offered to consumers, resulting in fewer choices and potentially higher prices.
[]. This high concentration, with HHI values above 2,000 and a delta of [400-450] which is
substantially above the threshold, further indicates SLC and also a risk of Lidl consolidating
its market position further. The Office considers that in the local geographic market:
a. Lidl is already leading and has a significant presence in the market, acquiring the Scotts
Zabbar store would further solidify the Lidl’s market share. This change would further
widen the gap between Lidl and its closest competitors, exacerbating the imbalance in
the competitive landscape.
b. Lidl’s market share has remained stable over the years, and thus, the acquisition would
further consolidate its high market share. Even a small increase in market share for a
strong player like Lidl could reinforce its strong position, reducing the competitive
pressures in the market. This is particularly important in the context that Lidl’s market
share has been stable over the years.
c. Lidl’s already high market share, combined with the addition of Scotts Zabbar’s market
share, would result in a market share that is appreciably larger than that of the largest
competitor. This would solidify Lidl’s market position and harm competition by making
155 RFI, dated 7th December 2023.
Office for Competition - 108 -

it harder for other competitors to challenge Lidl’s market presence effectively.
Considering Lidl’s high market shares that have remained stable over several years
this could indicate potential dominance.
d. The HHI and the delta increase resulting from this concentration are above the
thresholds set by the European Commission guidelines. This indicates an SLC. The
high HHI and delta values underscore the potential for reduced market competition in
the context of limited number of competitors, further justifying the rejection of Lidl’s
acquisition of the Scotts Zabbar store.
454. []. Even with Eurospin’s entry into the market, the SLC concerns would persist due to
Eurospin’s relatively low market share. Although Eurospin is a significant player in the
discount retail segment, its anticipated market share post-entry would not be sufficient to
counterbalance Lidl’s strong position. With Lidl’s market share expected to increase to []%
post-acquisition and the combined market share of competitors, including Eurospin, remaining
significantly lower, the competitive pressure exerted by Eurospin would be inadequate to
mitigate the anti-competitive effects of the acquisition. This imbalance would lead to reduced
competition, higher prices, fewer choices, and diminished quality of service for consumers in
the Zabbar and surrounding areas, reinforcing the Office’s concerns about the potential for
SLC even in the presence of Eurospin.
455. The GUPPI test suggests that the acquisition might reduce consumer welfare by allowing Lidl
the incentive to increase prices. Despite competitive offerings from other supermarkets, the
significant market concentration post-acquisition limits the extent to which these competitors
can constrain Lidl. Even with Eurospin’s potential entry in the local market, the market shares
would remain above []%, leading to a dominant position for Lidl.
456. Survey results show that 59.8% of Scotts (Zabbar) shoppers feel they would be worse off after
the acquisition, with only 14.7% expecting to benefit. Additionally, 70% of non-Lidl shoppers
believe the acquisition would negatively impact them. These findings suggest that consumers
do not view discounters and supermarkets as perfect substitutes, emphasising the negative
impact on consumer choice and welfare.
457. Discount retailers like Lidl often offer a limited selection of products at deeply discounted
prices, primarily private label brands. In contrast, traditional supermarkets like Scotts offer a
broader range of products, including branded items and additional services. This distinction
suggests that consumers who do not mainly shop at Lidl might be worse off due to the reduced
availability of traditional supermarkets, and even those who frequent Lidl might lose the option
to complement their shopping with traditional supermarkets.
458. The evidence also suggests that there is no sufficient number of other potential competitor/s
which could uphold sufficient competitive pressure post-transaction. The existing high market
shares of Lidl, pre- and post-concentration, assuming the presence of Eurospin, as well as its
intensions to expand further in the local geographic market and the lengthy process of
obtaining permits and developing a new supermarket and lack of swift alternative sites that
can be transformed in supermarket site within a reasonable amount of time imply that post-
concentration, Lidl would be strengthening its market position by precluding the possibility or
making it more difficult for other grocery retail markets to enter or expand.
459. The Office concludes that Lidl’s acquisition of Scotts in Zabbar leads to a SLC. The horizontal
unilateral effects and increased market concentration could harm both existing and future
competition, ultimately reducing consumer welfare and choice in the local grocery retail
market.

APPENDIX B - KEY INSIGHTS FROM SUPERMARKETS AND GROCERY STORES IN MALTA
Request for Information Results
Survey Instrument and Sample
In carrying out the assessment of this concentration, the Office for Competition gathered data from all
the undertakings operating in the grocery retail market in Malta by means of an RFI (Appendix A) in
accordance with Regulation 10 of the Control of Concentrations Regulations. The scope of this RFI was
to collect data which would assist the Office in delineating both the product and geographic markets
and establishing market shares. All undertakings contacted were asked a question on their sales area
and in cases where the sales area did not exceed 180 square meters, the questionnaire was terminated.
On the other hand, in cases where the sales area exceeded 180 square meters, undertakings were
asked to respond to a number of questions pertaining to turnover and the segregation between food
and non-food items, potential investments in the pipeline over the short-term, competitors, the prices of
a number of products, the availability of branded groceries, the product depth of a number of food and
non-food categories, their perception of brand substitutability with Lidl brands, and a number of
questions related to service including their weekly opening hours, whether they offer parking facilities,
online shopping, the number of checkout lanes, loyalty scheme programmes, and whether they offer
discounts as part of their promotion campaigns.
The RFI was sent on 23 November 2023 by email, where grocery retail outlets were asked to provide
their replies through an online form, to around 153 different grocery retail outlets (which include
supermarket chains).
Key Findings
Out of nearly 153 grocery retail outlets contacted via the RFI, 87 different grocery retail outlets (or that
are owned by 34 supermarkets chains composed of a number of outlets) have a gross sales floor area
exceeding the aforementioned threshold.156 As a result, these undertakings were requested to answer
all the questions that formed part of the RFI. The Office then compiled a database of all supermarket
chains and grocery retail outlets operating in Malta.
156 This figure was obtained from the two waves of data collected from the supply-side. The grocery retail outlets that failed to
respond to the Office’s RFI by the deadline set by the Office for Competition, where sent reminders and this data was then
collected in the subsequent weeks. Moreover, some of the grocery retail outlets to which the RFI was sent had closed their
business. Data was then cleaned and organised to correctly undertake the PQRS analysis and establish the relevant product
market. During this process, grocery retail outlets were contacted again for further clarifications on the provided data and to
supply any missing data in the RFI.

PQRS Analysis
The classification of stores (with a sales area of 200 square meters or more) as either being within or
outside the relevant product market are based on the PQRS analysis. The assessment of the Price,
Quality, Range and Service of the grocery retail outlets based on this store categorization helps to
gauge the extent of the competitive constraint imposed on the Notifying Party, as rational customers
typically choose between alternative stores by weighting the different stores characteristics included in
the PQRS analysis.
Price
The respondents were asked to provide the prices for 36 products. These included products such as
canned tuna, biscuits, butter, pasta, tomato paste, frozen vegetables, coffee, yoghurt, beer, coffee, soft
drinks, detergents, cleaning products and many others. The RFI asked for the prices of branded
products and included size specifications (in grams, millilitres, or quantity) to ensure comparability
between the prices charged by different stores. The products are listed in Table 2.
Each store’s reply to the questions on pricing was benchmarked against the average price of a selected
group of supermarkets (henceforth the ‘select group’) that are easily identified as direct competitors to
each other. These include the stores belonging to the Notifying Party (“Lidl” outlets), the stores
belonging to the Target (“Scotts” outlets), Smart Supermarket Ltd., PG Group (namely, PAVI
supermarket and PAMA supermarket), Greens supermarkets, and Welbee’s supermarkets (owned by
Retail Marketing Limited).
The “select group” was chosen by first analysing the results of the RFI responses on product
substitutability presented in the previous section. Most of the grocery retail outlets that the Office is
considering under the “select group” have stated that they consider their product categories to be
substitutable to the brands offered by Lidl outlets, thus emphasising the fact that for the “select group”,
Lidl is considered to be in direct competition in the market and thus imposing a competitive constraint
on the “select group”. Moreover, the “select group” comprises the most important market players in the
grocery retail sector.

Quality
For the quality assessment the Office does not produce a store classification analysis. The reason is
that the eighty-seven stores included in the PQRS assessment typically sell products with similar
brands. This means that the products sold by most stores are generally regarded by customers as being
of good and/or similar quality.
A notable exception is Lidl which sells which only sells a few products with similar brands to those sold
by other grocery retail outlets. Nonetheless, in a demand-side survey conducted by the Office in 2020
showed that 93% of Lidl’s customers either ‘strongly agree’ or ‘agree’ that Lidl’s products are of good
quality, even though their brands are not well known.160 Most of the product categories were highly
rated for their quality by customers, namely, refrigerated products, food cupboard items, beverages, pet
food, health and beauty products. This view is reinforced by the following demand-side survey results:
• 81.5% of Lidl’s customers either ‘strongly disagree’ or ‘disagree’ that Lidl’s products are of
inferior quality to branded products;
• 65.4% of Lidl’s customers either ‘strongly disagree’ or ‘disagree’ that Lidl’s products are of good
quality only in certain categories (such as drinks); and
• 94.3% of Lidl’s customers either ‘strongly agree’ or ‘agree’ that most of Lidl’s products are good.
On the basis of these results, the Office is of the opinion that quality matters for customers, as most
grocery outlets seem to offer good quality products in the eyes of the average customer, including Lidl.
Range
The respondents were asked to provide the product depth (in numbers) for 13 product groupings. These
products groups are listed in Table 4 and include oil, cereal and cereal bars, pasta, yoghurts and
custards, beers and ciders, health-related products, fresh vegetables, fresh meat, fresh fish, deli
counter, kitchen accessories, and pet-related products, as well as ironmongery products.161
A grocery retail outlet is deemed to impose a competitive constraint on the Notifying Party, i.e. Lidl, if
its range of products within a product grouping is at least as wide as that offered by the mean/minimum
of product range of the Notifying Party’s stores in at least 50% of the product groupings. Considering
that the sole Notifying Party involved in this concentration is Lidl, the mean number and the minimum

The rationale for this approach is as follows: If, for instance the Notifying Party’ outlets, which in this
case are all the Lidl outlets found across Malta,162 offer the lowest range of oil products and by definition
Lidl is part of the relevant market, then any other store that offers a range of oil products that is as
equally wide, or even wider than that offered by Lidl outlets, must also belong to the same product
market and thus is captures by the range component of the PQRS assessment.

Since stores may offer a range similar to that of the Notifying Party for certain categories but not for
others, the Office assesses stores to exert a competitive pressure on the Notifying Party only if their
product range matches or exceeds that of the minimum of the Notifying Party’s stores in at least 50%
of the product groupings (i.e., in at least 6 out of 12 product groupings). The 50% threshold was chosen
based on a series of sensitivity analyses to ensure that the results of the assessment are not
significantly influenced by minor variations in the selected threshold and align with expectations for
Malta’s major supermarkets.

The respondents were asked about the provision of several services that are generally deemed

service” characteristics is arbitrary. However, as was the case with the other classification criteria, the
Office subjected the threshold to a sensitivity analysis to ensure that the outcome of the analysis is not
highly sensitive to the arbitrarily chosen threshold.

On the basis of the PQRS analysis, each store is classified as either being within the relevant product
market or outside it. Those stores that impose a competitive constraint on the Notifying Party, in at least
two out of the three store characteristics (these being Price, Range and Service), are classified as being
part of the relevant market.163 As illustrated in the first column in Table 7 below, fifty-three out of
eighty-seven stores that have a sales area that is equal to or exceeds 200 square meters, are deemed
to form part of the relevant product market, which includes the larger supermarkets and Malta’s only
discounter, Lidl, but excludes convenience stores and some smaller and specialised stores.
The classification of stores necessarily entailed some degree of subjectivity. To ensure that the
classification based on the PQRS analysis yields a sensible outcome, we benchmark it against the
classification that we would have likely obtained had we based it on several headline indicators
(including annual turnover, average expenditure per customer, the percentage of sales accounted for
by food items and identification of competitors) that typically differ between stores that belong to
different relevant markets. The replies for each of the eighty-seven stores are presented in Table 7

three indicators together may be indicative of whether a specific store is likely to be part of the same

stores classified outside the relevant market in the same year. This disparity is also evident in the
average spend per customer, with stores classified as part of the relevant market reporting an average
spend per customer of €28, compared to only €16 for stores classified outside the relevant market.

have a significant proportion of their total turnover generated from food items. The data presented in

In the RFI sent to all grocery retail outlets, the Office provided the stores with a list of branded products
in various categories, such as groceries, frozen products, chilled products, confectionery products,
counter products, beverages and beers, cellar products, beauty products, health products, household
products, and pet products. The stores were then asked to provide data on which branded products
from these categories they sell at their respective outlets.174 These branded products are considered to
be overall of high quality.
Based on the responses received, the Office observes that larger supermarkets in the grocery retail
sector, particularly those in direct competition with the Notifying Party (Lidl), sell the majority of the
branded products listed. These supermarkets sell over 90% of the total 204 branded products across
the mentioned categories.
Furthermore, for stores classified within the relevant market, the proportion of these 204 branded
products sold varies from 66% to 98%. Notably, Lidl stands out among the stores classified within the
relevant market, selling an average of only []% of the listed 204 branded products across its 9 stores.
This percentage is significantly lower than the proportion sold by other outlets within the relevant market
and even lower than the total of branded products sold by the larger supermarkets.
This discrepancy can be attributed mainly to Lidl’s practice of offering and selling several unbranded
products imported and sold under the Lidl brand. This highlights the Office’s argument that Lidl stores
are categorised as discounters due to their distinctive product range offered in the market.
Additionally, the Office observed from the data on branded products gathered in the RFI that, in general,
convenience stores and the dedicated and specialized stores, which were excluded from the relevant
174 A total of 204 branded products.

product market based on the PQRS assessment conducted by the Office, offer a lower proportion of
the 204 branded products in their respective outlets compared to the larger supermarkets in the grocery
retail sector. This further supports the rationale behind the PQRS classification made by the Office in
its assessment of the relevant product market.
Furthermore, the Office finds it noteworthy that the percentage of branded products currently sold by
Lidl is even lower than that of most stores identifying themselves as convenience stores. This reinforces
the perception that Lidl stores exhibit more characteristics of discounters due to the limited number of
branded products they sell.
Data on online shopping was requested in the RFI, where respondents were asked whether they offer
online shopping to their customers and, if so, to state the proportion of their total turnover coming from
online sales. This inquiry was prompted by the fact that the Notifying Party does not offer online
shopping services. Additionally, given the exceptional circumstances brought about by the Covid-19
pandemic since 2020, the Office sought to analyse whether this has impacted online shopping trends
in the grocery retail market in recent years.
Based on the data provided by the grocery retail outlets, the Office estimates that the total proportion
of online shopping as a percentage of total turnover for stores with a sales area of 200 square meters
or more was 1.3% in 2020. This rate increased to 2.3% in 2021 and further to 2.9% in 2022. Although
there has been an increase in online shopping over the past three years, primarily due to the impact of
the Covid-19 pandemic, it is not considered an exponential increase, as the ratio of online shopping to
physical shopping at these stores remains negligible.
Furthermore, the Office assesses the proportion of online shopping attributed to stores classified within
and outside the relevant market. As shown in Table 11 below, stores classified within the relevant
market have a higher proportion of online shopping turnover compared to those classified outside the
relevant market. This trend has continued to increase in favour of stores classified within the relevant
market from 2020 to 2022. Based on the results obtained from the RFI data, the Office does not consider
it necessary to treat online shopping as a separate market from in-store shopping.

APPENDIX D – CONSUMER BEHAVIOUR AND PERCEPTIONS IN THE MALTESE GROCERY
RETAIL MARKET – INSIGHTS FROM SURVEY FINDINGS
This box presents the findings derived from an exit-store survey conducted as part of the Office for
Competition's assessment into Lidl's proposed acquisition of Scotts Zabbar. The survey was conducted
from the 18th of January till the 4th of February 2024 and involved brief exit interviews conducted at
Scotts Zabbar, targeting customers who had just completed purchases at the supermarket checkouts.
The questionnaire comprises primary demographic characteristics, consumer supermarket shopping
habits and preferences and delves into the perceptions regarding the anticipated effects of the new Lidl
store.
Fieldwork was carried out by Sagalytics on behalf of the Office.
The sample data consists of 401 grocery shoppers. The below analysis is not treated for outliers and
no adjustments to the data was made.
1. Overview of Customers
• Around two thirds of customers were women and a third were men.
• Around 75% of the shoppers were aged 45 and over.

2. Overview of Customers
Shopping at Scotts Zabbar
• Most of the respondents replied that they do their main grocery shopping from Scotts Zabbar,
mainly due to its convenient location. Indeed, 72% of the shoppers came to the store from
home, with the preferred mode of transport being the car and actual travel time taking mostly 5
and 10 minutes.
• Apart from this, shoppers also chose to shop from Scotts Zabbar given the wide variety of
products available.
• More than half of the respondents stated that they would have still done their shopping at Scotts
Zabbar even if the prices increased by 5%.
Online Shopping
• Online grocery shopping is still not prevalent in Malta, with 93% of the respondents claiming
that they did not do any online shopping in the last 3 months.
• Furthermore, 77% of these stated that they do not consider substituting, even partially, the
traditional way of supermarket grocery shopping with online shopping.
Office for Competition - 152 -

• Of the 7% that stated that they have shopped online in the last 3 months, the main online
shopping items related to preservatives, fridge and bakery items, laundry products and fresh
fruit and vegetables.
• The respondents mainly do their online shopping from Greens and PG Group, with Scotts also
being an online favourite shop.

Expectations of respondents that shop at Lidl
• 82% of those that shop at Lidl stated that they would consider to start doing their Lidl shopping
at the new Lidl Zabbar store instead of the Lidl store they currently shop from.
• Similarly, 82% of those that stated that they shop at Lidl claimed that they would consider
purchasing from another supermarket now that Scotts Zabbar will become a Lidl Supermarket.
The preferred choice among the respondents being Pavi (Qormi) and Chain (Fgura).
• Only 8% of those that stated that they shop at Lidl claimed that they would consider purchasing
from another Scotts Supermarket now that Scotts Zabbar will become a Lidl Supermarket,
mainly from Scotts St. Lucija.
Expectations of Respondents that do not shop at Lidl
Of the 35% of the respondents that claimed that they do not shop at Lidl:
• 54% stated that they would consider buying from a different supermarket once Scotts Zabbar
is transferred to a Lidl Outlet. The preferred alternative supermarkets being Pavi (Qormi),
Greens (Mriehel) and Chain (Fgura).
• 25% stated that they would consider purchasing from Lidl Zabbar.
Expectations of new Lidl Zabbar
• 50.4% of the respondents claim that they are going to be worse-off now that Scotts Zabbar will
be transferred into Lidl.
• 20.4% of the respondents claim that they would be better-off with a new Lidl Zabbar.
